title: D-Wave shows off its new entry in quantum computing race
gist: D-Wave, historically known for quantum annealing, published a Nature paper demonstrating fast (500ns) high-fidelity entanglement between two dual-rail qubits acquired via its acquisition of Yale spinout Quantum Circuits — the same 'erasure qubit' approach used by Amazon — while acknowledging unresolved error-rate scaling and mid-circuit detection problems, with a roadmap to 181 dual-rail qubits by 2028.

themes.theme: D-Wave's strategic pivot into gate-based quantum computing

insights.claim: D-Wave, founded in the last century, built its original business on quantum annealing — a non-general-purpose machine for solving optimization problems — distinct from gate-based quantum computers being developed by IBM or Google.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: D-Wave's historical annealer-only positioning limited its addressable market versus general-purpose quantum computing rivals; this context frames why the gate-based pivot is strategically significant.

insights.claim: A few years ago D-Wave began developing gate-based hardware using an unusual qubit technology called fluxonium, and this year acquired a startup called Quantum Circuits — spun out of Yale University — which had been developing 'dual-rail qubits,' the same technology used by Amazon.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: D-Wave acquiring rather than organically developing dual-rail expertise is a build-via-M&A strategy in quantum computing; investors should track whether this consolidation trend continues as smaller quantum startups get absorbed by larger players.

insights.claim: Dual-rail qubits promise to make most errors very easy to detect (as photon loss, termed an 'erasure qubit'), simplifying the error-correction overhead required to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: If the erasure-qubit approach holds up at scale, it could require substantially less hardware overhead per logical qubit than competing error-correction architectures — a key efficiency thesis for evaluating D-Wave's hardware roadmap against competitors like IBM, Google, and Amazon.

themes.theme: Nature paper: validating entanglement without breaking the error hierarchy

insights.claim: D-Wave published a paper in Nature demonstrating that two dual-rail qubits can be entangled without altering their best feature — that most errors remain a single, easily detectable type (photon loss).
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Peer-reviewed publication in Nature is a credibility marker that lends independent scientific validation to D-Wave's technical claims, relevant for assessing the company's R&D credibility versus promotional claims.

insights.claim: In the dual-rail qubit hierarchy, photon loss (escape from the hardware) was the dominant error type, phase flips were the next most common, and bit flips were a very distant third — and D-Wave's two-qubit entangling gate preserved this same error hierarchy rather than distorting it, which the company called a key achievement.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Preserving the error hierarchy during two-qubit operations (rather than introducing new dominant error types) is the technical prerequisite for D-Wave's simplified error-correction thesis to actually work at scale — this is the paper's central validating result.
insights.quote: Often when you start producing two qubit or entangling gates, you can distort your error hierarchy. So for dominant errors, things other than erasures can start cropping in.

insights.claim: The entangling gate operation was fast: activating the connection, waiting about 200 nanoseconds, then shutting it off, with the entire entanglement process taking 500 nanoseconds total.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Sub-microsecond entangling gate speed is a concrete, comparable performance metric against other qubit modalities (superconducting transmon, trapped ion, etc.) for benchmarking D-Wave's hardware against competitors.

insights.claim: Photon loss rates were about 0.5 percent per entanglement operation and were five times more common than any other error type, while bit-flips were 'practically non-existent at the 10^-6 level,' per the paper; most losses affected the source (control) qubit.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A 0.5% loss rate and near-zero bit-flip rate are specific quantitative benchmarks that quantum computing analysts can use to compare D-Wave's dual-rail fidelity against rival architectures' published error rates.
insights.quote: Bit-flips are practically non-existent at the 10−6 level.

insights.claim: The devices showed rising error rates as more operations were performed, with the paper acknowledging an 'unexpected approximately quadratic decrease' in fidelity and purity as gate count increases, attributed to possible drift in calibration parameters or frequency fluctuations in the coupling transmon.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Quadratic (not linear) error scaling with operation count is a meaningful scaling problem that could limit how many sequential operations are practically achievable before error correction becomes overwhelmed — a key open technical risk for D-Wave's roadmap.
insights.quote: As the number of gates increases, both the fidelity and purity of the final state exhibit an unexpected approximately quadratic decrease.

insights.claim: Mid-circuit erasure (photon-loss) detection — measuring for errors while a calculation is still in progress, not just at the end — is still a work in progress for D-Wave, according to Lanting, even though other quantum computing technologies have already demonstrated this capability.
insights.speaker: Trevor Lanting (via John Timmer)
insights.so_what: D-Wave is behind competing quantum hardware approaches on a capability (mid-circuit measurement) that is necessary for practical fault-tolerant computation, indicating a gap versus more mature rival architectures despite D-Wave's favorable error hierarchy.
insights.quote: We are working on techniques for doing mid-circuit erasure detection. We don’t have this perfected yet, but we’ve got ideas and a plan and a roadmap for detecting these, not just at the end but as you’re running your circuit.

insights.claim: Interpreting the error 'syndrome' data from a logical qubit requires substantial classical compute, and this challenge grows when error classes differ greatly in frequency; Lanting expects the dual-rail approach's richer information stream can help reduce this classical computational burden, though it remains an open theoretical problem.
insights.speaker: Trevor Lanting (via John Timmer)
insights.so_what: The classical-compute overhead for decoding quantum error syndromes is an underappreciated cost center in quantum computing economics — an open question that affects total system cost, not just qubit count, when evaluating any quantum hardware roadmap.

insights.claim: D-Wave plans to reach 181 dual-rail qubits by 2028, which the company believes should provide enough time to test several forms of the surface code error-detection scheme; beyond that, the challenge becomes making and linking enough hardware to host a hundred or more logical (error-corrected) qubits.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A concrete numeric roadmap milestone (181 physical dual-rail qubits by 2028) gives investors and technologists a specific, falsifiable checkpoint to evaluate D-Wave's execution against stated goals, and to compare pace against IBM, Google, and other quantum roadmaps.

insights.claim: Amazon's dual-rail approach differs from D-Wave's in that Amazon mediates any connection between dual-rail qubits through an intervening transmon-based qubit, meaning it never has to directly entangle dual-rail qubits — unlike D-Wave's approach demonstrated in this paper.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: This is a specific architectural divergence between two companies pursuing the same underlying erasure-qubit concept, giving investors a concrete technical axis (direct entanglement vs. mediated coupling) on which to compare D-Wave's and Amazon's competing quantum computing bets.
